question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?
summary: Ensemble signals a high likelihood (94%) of increasing the settlement qualifying period to 10 years by May 2026.
Adversarial objections identify credible risks from consultation outcomes, transitional rules, and political opposition that could delay adoption.
Threshold analysis and public policy momentum suggest a near-term move is plausible, but not guaranteed within the May 2026 window.
Overall calibration favors a high likelihood with meaningful downward risk from procedural and political uncertainties.

justification.critique_assessment: Objections are valid and reveal a genuine risk of delay due to consultation outcomes, transitional arrangements, and political opposition.
justification.adjustment: Adjusted downward from 0.94 to 0.88 to account for credible delay risks identified in the objections, while maintaining the general trajectory toward a 10-year baseline by May 2026.

forecasts.reference-class: UK immigration settlement reforms moving from a fixed five-year ILR path to a ten-year baseline under the Earned Settlement framework, with potential transitional arrangements and a consultation period (Nov 2025–Feb 2026) and proposed implementation from April 2026.

sources.claim: The government published an earned settlement consultation proposing replacing the five-year route with a ten-year baseline and a merit-based earned settlement; consultation open until 12 February 2026.
Accessible summary of the earned settlement proposal describes a 10-year baseline and the framework for earned settlement.
The Commons Library notes that immigration rules would begin to change from April 2026, subject to the consultation outcome.
Hill Dickinson outlines the earned settlement proposals, including a 10-year baseline and abolition of the 10-year long residence route, with the consultation closing 12 February 2026.
DavidsonMorris summarises earned settlement with a baseline 10-year period and potential transitional features; notes no rules have changed yet.
Electronic Immigration Network reports that the White Paper proposed doubling the standard qualifying period from five to ten years.
The government announced in Nov 2025 that the permanent settlement qualifying period would be doubled to 10 years.
House of Commons Library notes that the 10-year baseline settlement period will begin to apply from April 2026, with transitional arrangements.
The 'A Fairer Pathway to Settlement' speech states that the starting point for settlement will move from 5 years to 10.
The Earned Settlement consultation discusses options including increasing the baseline to 10 years (with possible reductions for certain contributions).
Guardian reports that the white paper would double the wait for many migrants to 10 years for permanent settlement.
Guardian reports IPPR analysis that ministers intend to extend the settlement period to 10 years, potentially affecting hundreds of thousands of children.

The default qualifying period for settlement will be increased from five years to ten years under the Earned Settlement consultation, with a time-adjustment model and four pillars (character, integration, contribution, residence) affecting reductions.

The government announced on 20 November 2025 that the baseline qualifying period would be ten years, with some cohorts able to qualify earlier (e.g., high-skill roles, NHS/public service) and a public consultation to shape details.
Debate notes indicate a baseline ten-year path for settlement with exceptions and potential faster routes for certain groups; proposal is subject to consultation.

The Earned Settlement framework would generally extend waiting periods for most migrants to around ten years, with a public consultation open through February 2026; the measure is part of broader reforms to settlement pathways.
Reporting on the government’s proposals to tighten settlement rules and raise waiting times, including a baseline 10-year period with longer waits for some cohorts.

synthesis: The consensus points to a strong move to a 10-year baseline, but credible delays from consultations, transitional rules, and opposition temper the near-term certainty. For calibration, I adjust the probability down from 0.94 to 0.88 to reflect these non-physics-based delays while preserving the overall trajectory toward a 10-year baseline by May 2026.
